segments.text: Hello, I'm Norman Swan and welcome to this week's Health Report. Today on the programme, we offer sucker to the sore knee. We offer reduced worries to women undergoing IVF. We take a hard look at Xanax and persistently large variations in preventable hospital admissions in Australia, particularly looking at Queensland and Victoria. This is a report just released from the Grattan Institute in Melbourne. Stephen Duckett's the Health Programme Director and he joins us from the studio in Melbourne. Welcome Stephen.
Good afternoon, Norman.
So this is about place.
I mean, just describe the study to us
because these are extraordinary variations
where some parts of Australia,
particularly in Queensland and Victoria,
38 places in Queensland, 25 places in Victoria,
have a 50% increased average hospitalisations
that are preventable,
and they've lasted for over a decade.
Yes, so we got all of the hospital data
for Queensland and Victoria,
and we analysed, we decided there'd be a threshold of 50% worse than the state average.
We used the list of so-called ambulatory care sensitive conditions
or potentially preventable hospitalisations.
So these are ones that just ambulatory care is code for.
They could be treated by your GP in the community.
That's right. That's right.
And so we used the list that had been agreed by governments.
And so we started by trying to identify those places which had high rates.
What we found was that an area with a high rate in one year has a 50% chance of being not a high rate the next year.
Really?
So we were quite interested in the extent of persistence that we've got to actually see if something's going to have a place that's got a high rate for three years or more, it's likely to stay.
Whereas if it's only one year, it's not likely to stay high.
So then we were even tougher and said, we're interested in those areas which have had high rates every year for a decade.
And it surprised us we found these places that have, this is supposed to be potentially preventable hospitalisations,
where they're more than 50% above the state average every year for a decade.
So what sort of places are we talking about? Are these surprises?
Well, yes and no.
So we found places in metropolitan areas and in rural areas, remote areas.
So some of the Aboriginal communities, Palm Island and so on, Arrakoon, have got high rates.
Lower socioeconomic status areas in the suburbs, like Caboolture in Brisbane or Broadmeadows in Melbourne, also have high rates.
But what was quite interesting about this, we went in saying,
oh, look, all the low socioeconomic status areas
are going to have high rates
of potentially preventable hospitalisations.
But that turned out not to be the case.
So in Melbourne, for example...
So it wasn't just about poverty.
It wasn't just about poverty.
So in Melbourne, Broadmeadows has got a high rate
of potentially preventable hospitalisations
every year for a decade.
Sunshine never had a high rate
of potentially preventable hospitalisations.
And Frankston, which is a bit richer, does too.
Yes, so it's quite mixed.
They're individual...
And we also looked at differences in patterns.
So in some of these places, a small number of people who have high rates of readmission
drive the problem.
But in other places, it's not readmissions at all, even though many of these are chronic
diseases.
So it's a very localized issue and quite different in different parts of Australia.
And what sort of conditions are we talking about here?
So the standard sort of list of chronic diseases,
angina, diabetes, asthma,
but also some acute conditions like dental care,
admissions for dental care are also in our list.
And extraordinary variations in dental care.
Well, it's quite extraordinary.
So generally, in fact, if you look again at Melbourne,
in metropolitan Melbourne,
none of the postcodes had high rates of admissions for dental care.
But in parts of rural Victoria,
there are places which two or three times the state average.
So Colac, for example, not a poor area.
Mildura have more than twice the state average rate of admission for dental care.
So presumably for extractions.
Extractions, gum disease possibly.
And it's probably because neither of those places have had fluoride for very long.
They basically fluoridated in 2010 in both of those cases.
And so the community didn't have the public health intervention that they should have had in terms of fluoridated in the water supply.
So that's one cause.
You call these hotspots and maintained heat in many ways over a 10-year period.
What are the other factors that differentiate an area that looks very similar on paper yet doesn't have this unacceptably high unnecessary hospitalisation rate?
Well, all we can analyse is the outcome, that is the hospitalisation, and occasionally we can look at the readmissions and so on.
But we actually don't know whether it's because there's just no primary care there or very poor primary care access,
or because the primary care is there and is good, but the disease burden is so high.
We try to look at the access to primary care.
So this is general practice.
General practice.

Yeah, so we asked for Medicare data to enable us to look at age, sex, standardised rates of admission by geographic area, but we weren't allowed access to those data, so we couldn't actually look at the…
I thought the Commonwealth had this new policy that data were open to walls with the aim of better health through data.
That's our hope too, Norman.
But we were given data with age and sex in it, and we're given data with geography in it, but not neither twain should meet.
So we couldn't do standardised grants.
So the new era of open data has not quite arrived.
Not quite in time for our study.
So given you don't know what the causes are, how do you know what the solutions are?
So what we're saying is the action has to be at the local level.
And the new organisations that have been created with Commonwealth funding, the primary healthcare networks, in our view,
or they're required by the Commonwealth to set priorities about what they should be doing.
And we're suggesting that those organisations need to set priorities for these places which
have had such disadvantage for 10 years in a row. They should be investigating what is it
that's in the local community? What is it that's not there? What is it that's causing these,
that's driving these admissions? And they should be developing local action. And also,
we should be evaluating that. There should be a national evaluation of what's happening in
these places because we've got to learn from each place to another place because the intervention
strategies, what needs to be done, isn't well known and we don't have a good evidence base for that.
And given it's place-based, it's going to be different for different communities?
Yes, there may be some commonalities. So, you know, these are chronic diseases and so you might
say, well, do they have in place self-management programs to teach people how to manage their own
chronic disease better? And does that make a difference?
And does that make a difference?
Well, the evidence is it sort of does,
but we actually haven't tried that.
We haven't evaluated in the various,
does it work in an Aboriginal community?
Does it work in a suburban Melbourne
or suburban Brisbane and so on?
Well, we watch with interest.
Stephen Duckett, thanks for joining us on The Health Report.
Thanks, Norman.
Professor Stephen Duckett,
who's Health Program Director at the Grattan Institute
and that report's available on their website.
And you're listening to The Health Report here
on Radio National, ABC News Radio and CBC Radio in Canada.
Welcome to all our Canadian listeners.
For many years now, there's been fears and conflicting evidence that in vitro fertilization
might increase the risk of breast cancer in women undergoing the procedure.
Now, a large 20-year study has come up with what many hope are definitive answers.
One of the authors of the study is Alexander van der Belduisabert,
and she's in the Department of Epidemiology at the Netherlands Cancer Institute,
and she joins me on the line from Holland.
Welcome to The Health Report, Alexandra.
Hello, good morning.
Why might IVF cause breast cancer?
Female sex hormone levels increase during in vitro fertilization,
during the ovarian stimulation that is necessary for retrieving eggs.
And sex hormone levels have been known to increase the risk of breast cancer.
So you're not using estrogen to stimulate the ovaries,
but they use hormones that stimulate the ovaries,
and then the ovaries produce estrogen and then that drives the breasts.
That's the theory.
Yes, exactly.
And what evidence before your study was there that there might be a risk?
There had been many studies,
but the drawback was that the studies were limited in numbers of breast cancer
and the follow-up was too short to be sure what would be the risk in long term.
But it's not just increased hormone levels.
When you do IVF, you also decrease the hormone levels, don't you,
to actually take control of the menstrual cycle?
Yes, that's true.
First, the cycle, first the levels are decreased,
and after that, the ovarian stimulation takes place and the levels increase.
So what did you do in this study?
um we had 25 000 women that had been treated for subfertility problems 19 000 ivf treated women
in the period 1983 to 1995 and also 6 000 women who received other subfertility treatments
in roughly the same period so you're comparing so you're comparing ivf but you're also comparing
women with infertility per se to see whether infertility itself had an influence on breast
cancer yes exactly we followed all these women through december 2013 that was a median follow-up
of 21 years and we compared both groups with the general population in the netherlands and we
compared the ivf group with the non-ivf group and what did you find we found that the risk was not
increased, neither compared to the general population or with the non-IVF group, not
even when the follow-up was more than 20 years.
And there was also not a difference for the different types of treatment or different
types of sub-fetility diagnosis.
On reading your paper, it looked as though the more IVF cycles, I mean, you don't want
women have unnecessary IVF cycles, but the more IVF cycles a woman had,
the less likely she was to develop breast cancer.
What's going on there?
Yes, women who received more than six cycles of IVF
and also women who had a low egg yield at the first IVF cycle
had a decreased risk.
And that can be explained because those women tend to reach menopause
at an earlier age and an earlier age of menopause protects or decreases the risk of breast cancer.
Which is also a story about estrogen stimulation because the more menstrual cycles you have,
the more estrogen stimulation you have and therefore later onset of menstruation in your
life and earlier cessation of menstruation decreases the risk of breast cancer. So that
was nothing to do with IVF, that was simply a phenomenon of those women who were particularly
who were reaching the end of their fertile life a bit earlier than you might have expected.
Yes, exactly.
And that was exactly the reason,
probably the reason that they had to go for IVF to still have a pregnancy.
Now, ovarian stimulation isn't quite so aggressive these days,
but presumably that's not the reason.
It's presumably to improve outcomes.
So although these studies are not cause and effect, there are associations because you're just looking at the relationship between factors over time.
Can you be confident in saying to women now, look, it really doesn't look likely that breast cancer is a risk of IVF?
Yes, these results are quite reassuring for women who have been treated with IVF in the past.
And since the treatments have been quite similar in the different Western countries,
we also have confidence that the results are applicable to other Western countries.
What about other female cancers, such as cancer of the uterus, endometrial cancer or ovarian cancer?
Yes. In our study, we are also looking into the risks of other hormone-related cancers.
And we recently did analyses on melanoma and colorectal cancer, and we didn't find increased risks either.
And we are also in the future investigating the risks of endometrial cancer and ovarian cancer.
and we will do that in an even larger cohort
because we recently also included women
who have been treated in the period 1995 to 2000.
So then we have more than 40,000 women in the cohort.
So, Cosfer, and we'll just follow that up
and hopefully speak to you when you've got some results there
before we set any panic afoot.
Luke, thank you very much for joining us, Alexandra.
Okay, thank you.
Alexander van den Belk-Dusabout, who's in the Department of Epidemiology at the Netherlands
Cancer Institute. And as I say, you're listening to The Health Report here on Radio National,
CBC Radio and ABC News Radio. For a long time, there's been an ongoing controversy when you're
middle-aged and have a torn knee cartilage of whether it's worth doing an arthroscopy,
which is telescope surgery, minimal invasive surgery to actually trim the cartilage. You

it was more arthritis than torn meniscus or a torn cartilage.

of comparing exercise therapy to arthroscopy
for people who've had a meniscal tear or a torn cartilage.
And on the line from Martina Hansen's hospital in Norway

Welcome to the Health Report.
Hello. Hello to you.
Tell me about this study.
Oh, the study, yes. We had 140 patients, and half of them has gone through arthroscopic partial meniskectomy, and the other half has gone through exercise therapy.
All patients had degenerative meniscus tears in their meniscus and had pain in the joint line.
And we took X-rays at baseline and only 4% of them had osteoarthritis evaluated by X-rays.
So there have been some studies earlier comparing these patients doing exercise therapy or exercise therapy in addition to surgery.
And the conclusion has been that surgery has no additional effect in these patients.
So let's just double back for a moment because you've given away the punchline very early, Nina, but thank you very much for doing that.
So what I covered, in fact, recently was arthritis.
So if you've got arthritis and your knee surgeon says, look, I'm going to clean it out with arthroscopy, there's no advantage to that versus dummy.
No, it's not.
No, not in the long term.
So when somebody has, you know, some people say that a tail-torn cartilage is, in fact, a normal phenomenon of aging.
but the people that you looked at
and whether or not you've got symptoms or not
but the people that you looked at actually had symptoms

they had pain in the knee
that's why they went to their

and
they saw that

practiced

This is older people.

The exercise program consisted of warming up exercises,
strengthening exercises and neuromuscular the exercises for balance so the and then so just

what do they do they were standing at bosu balls do you know what that is yeah uh doing uh knee

they there was no difference in any symptoms no it was not not not after two
years what is the main outcome of this study now you are but but did they both
get improvement? The exercise group improved in muscle strength at three months and 12 months.
Did they both improve with pain? Yes, they did. Now, you allowed people after they'd been in the
exercise group to cross over. If they were unhappy, they could go off and have knee surgery,
they could often have knee arthroscopy, and one in five of them did. What happened to them?
Yes. They were, after two years of follow-up, they were exactly like the other patients.
so they did not lose anything by going through exercise therapy first.
And the other way of looking at that is they didn't gain anything

No, no, no, they didn't actually.
So I'm right, Nina, you are an orthopedic surgeon.
Yes.
So are your colleagues talking to you anymore?
Yes, they do.
So they don't feel that you've undermined the knee surgery market in Norway?
No, not at all.
There has been a slow decrease in arthroscopy for these patients
the last two years in Norway, as also seen in Denmark and Sweden.
And I think that is a result of the RCTs that have been published the last year.
the one that I mentioned earlier and also the one from Finland by Sivon who

But what you didn't do was do nothing.
Have you got any sense of you've got a meniscal tear,
you've got a bit of pain, well, why bother doing anything?

No, I'm sorry for that.

So that's a weakness of our study,
that we had no group without treatment at all.
That's the plan for me further on now,
to look on patients coming to our hospital.
and I will follow them and take them back after two or five years
to see how they come out if they have not done the exercise therapy

So if they are not in the study, I think many patients

So not content with destroying the orthopaedic industry in Norway, you're going to go after the physiotherapist and it's as physiologist.
I'm glad to hear it.
But no doubt the accountants in the Norwegian Department of Health are delighted with you.
Look, Nina Kajs, thank you very much for joining us.

Thank you very much indeed.
Yes, thank you.
Nina Keis is an orthopedic surgeon at Martina Hansen's Hospital in Sandvik in Norway, listening to the health report here on RN.
Now, there's a drug, an anti-anxiety drug around called Xanax.
Many of you have heard about it.
It's actually quite toxic.
And the government realized that it was fairly toxic.
Lots of calls to the poison center.
And they rescheduled it.
and there's been a study done at the University of New South Wales,
the colleagues at the University of Sydney,
looking at what the effect of rescheduling those drugs are
because how do you actually change the way drugs are prescribed and influenced
and can regulation actually have an influence?
And the person doing that study along with her colleagues is Andrea Schaefer
who's in the unit of Big Data Research and Health at the University of New South Wales.
Welcome to the Health Report.
Thank you very much, Norman.
Big Data Research and Health.
Just tell us about your unit before we get on to the subject of Xanax.
Well, we primarily do research that uses data that has been collected for reasons other than research purposes, so administrative data.
For example, in the study that we did, we used pharmaceutical benefit scheme data on pharmacy claims that have been dispensed at chemists,
and hospitalization data collected at the state level, as well as emergency department data.
Medicare benefits scheme data as well.
So you've been sitting listening to the program

from the Commonwealth.
Yes.
Did you?
It can...

Because the Commonwealth is boasting about how the fact

Yes, I think there's something coming up in the pipeline,

to get access to data.
Right.
And sometimes when you talk about big data in health,
people are using other data that are not in health at all, like supermarket data or people's
shopping habits and things like that. Do you use that in your research too? I'm not aware of anyone
in our group who uses that sort of data. No, at this stage, it's mostly health data. So let's talk
about Xanax. What's the problem with Xanax? The actual proper name for it is Alprazolam. It is,
yes. Well, Alprazolam, when it's compared to other benzodiazepines... It's used for anxiety and panic
disorder. Anxiety and insomnia as well. Although in Australia, it's only PBS listed for the treatment
of panic disorder. Compared to other benzodiazepines, alprazolam, it's more toxic and as well,
it's more commonly abused. And its use had been increasing in Australia. And so that was concerning.
And that is why the TGA decided to reschedule it. And what was the toxicity? Well, when
individuals might overdose on a benzodiazepine, if they're taking alprazolam, they're more likely
to die or have worse outcomes than if they overdose on, say, diazepam or oxazepam.
And was it being abused as well?
Yes, it's commonly abused, particularly by people who abuse opioids, for example, heroin.
And patients who overdose on illicit drugs, they're often also abusing alprazolam.
So if you're on alprazolam and you're on, say, heroin, that could increase your risk
of dying of an overdose simply because of the two drugs working together? Yes, yeah, and in comparison
to say other benzodiazepines. So when they rescheduled, what did they actually do? Well,
in Australia, all medicines are classified into a schedule and the majority of medicines that
are prescribed, such as statins or blood pressure medicines, they're classified as schedule four.
Which means that the GP can just write an ordinary script for them. Exactly. Medicines that have a
high potential for abuse or addiction, they're classified as Schedule 8, and those are called
controlled drugs. So morphine-like drugs would be on Schedule 8? Exactly, yes. And so what that
means is that those medicines, they can still be prescribed, but they're just subject to additional
restrictions and controls. Such as? The restrictions vary by state, but includes things like getting a
permit from a state authority to prescribe, requiring that the GP handwrite the prescription,
and having the prescriptions expire after six months rather than a year.
So it just becomes much more difficult.
It does, yes.
And what did you do in this study?
Well, we had access to...
I mean, is there any doubt that rescheduling changes prescribing habits?
I mean, it would make sense that it does.
Yeah, that's what you'd expect.
But the issue is not only does it reduce prescribing of alprazolam,
but we also want to look at whether there's any unintended consequences,
either positive or negative.
For example, if alprazolam is more difficult to get, are people switching to other less appropriate drugs or are they switching to more appropriate alternatives?
Given that the evidence base for these drugs treating anxiety disorders is pretty poor in the first place.
Yes.
What did you find?
Well, we found that almost immediately after the rescheduling, the prescribing of alprazolam dropped by 22%.
And there were a lot of prescriptions, like 18,000 or something.
Yes, we had over a study period, which was six years.
Oh, so it's over six years.
Yeah, there was 18,000 people in our sample.
So this is a 10% sample of all prescribed oprahazolam in Australia.
And that was 18,000 people over six years.
So it's still quite a large number if it's a 10% sample.
Yes, yeah.
So the prescribing dropped by 22%.
We also found that there was increases in the use of other less toxic benzodiazepines,
particularly oxazepam and diazepam.
Diazepam, which the common trade name is Valium.
Yes.
So there was a trade-off.
Was it a one-to-one trade-off or did the overall rate of prescribing of benzodiazepines,
which is actually what you'd want, you'd want that to go down, did it overall go down
or was it a one-to-one trade-off?
It's a bit difficult to compare.
One of the issues is Alprazolam, well, all medicines can be prescribed and dispensed
privately as well as through the PBS.
And we only had access to PBS prescriptions.
So the GPs might have reverted to private prescriptions.
Well, it could be also...
But it was still Schedule 8, so you've still got rules about the private prescription.
Exactly, yeah.
So we suspect that the private market would have acted similarly to the PBS market,
but you may have people switching from the private or praslan market
into the PBS diazepam market, for example.
And calls to the poison centre halved.
They did.
So over 12 months after the rescheduling, they dropped by 50%.
And probably most importantly,
we didn't see any increases in calls for poison aids associated with other benzodiazepines or

so we didn't identify any increases in adverse outcomes um given the data that we had and the
